title: Stooping to the Weak
english: …the use of foods. But for those who have not yet come to this judgment, these things are not yet clean, by what seems right to them; they are common, because their mind somehow limps on the way to the truth.

“So do not let your good be spoken of as evil” (Romans 14:16). Let not the brilliance of those who are well approved lift itself up over the weak, nor let your good, that is, what is admirable in your faith, be spoken ill of by anyone. For the achievements of a life pleasing to God would not come about through eating (Romans 14:17), nor would such a person be worthy of the kingdom of heaven, as one who reveres God, if he eats without distinction whatever is set before him; rather, the one who is worthy is he who stoops to the weakness of his weak brothers and abstains.

For even if Paul blamed Peter for living like a Jew because of those who had come to Antioch from James (Galatians 2:11–14), he did not blame him for stooping to the weakness of those of the circumcision and abstaining from foods. He blamed him because, by the weight of his own standing, he was drawing the many believers from the nations into thinking that they had to live according to the law, and Paul’s preaching was in danger of coming to nothing; for he was the teacher of the nations.
“All things indeed are clean, but it is wrong for the one who eats and gives offence” (Romans 14:20).
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: u10-rem-close ends ἀνεῖται δὲ πάντως ἐπ' ἐξουσίας τῶν ('is left wholly at the free disposal ... the'), and this section supplies ἐδωδίμων ἡ χρῆσις ('the use of foods'). The leading ellipsis marks the join.

κατὰ τὸ αὐτοῖς δοκοῦν ἔχειν ὀρθῶς: 'according to what seems to them to be right'; Cyril applies Romans 14:14 (to the one who reckons a thing common, it is common), which was the lemma of u10-rem-close.

After the lemma the copy-text has a broken οὐ γάρ followed by a fresh sentence (Μὴ κατεπαιρέσθω ...); the same words οὐ γὰρ open the sentence after next. Taken as a false start or dittography in the copy-text and not translated; nothing else is omitted.
ἀλλ' ὁ συγκαταβαίνων: the predicate 'worthy' is carried over from the preceding clause; English supplies 'the one who is worthy is he who'.
εἰ ἀδιακρίτως ἐσθίει τὰ παρατιθέμενα: possible echo of 1 Corinthians 10:27 (πᾶν τὸ παρατιθέμενον ὑμῖν ἐσθίετε); noted only.

ἐμέμψατο: the subject is Paul, named in English; αὐτῷ τὸ κήρυγμα is likewise Paul's preaching, since he 'was the teacher of the nations' (cf. 1 Timothy 2:7, διδάσκαλος ἐθνῶν; possible echo, noted only).
τῷ ἀξιοπίστῳ τοῦ προσώπου ἑαυτοῦ: 'by the credibility of his own person', rendered 'by the weight of his own standing'.
διὰ προσκόμματος ἐσθίοντι: 'eating through (with) stumbling'; rendered 'eats and gives offence', the sense Cyril draws out in u11-rem-early.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u11 open
